meta.title: What We Built: The Config-Instantiated Parser Pipeline
meta.description: How the NAAC intent pipeline went from hardcoded sequence to policy-driven instrument — and why that was the real answer to the say-again problem

props.title: From Hardcoded Sequence to Policy Instrument
props.subtitle: What we actually built when we set out to build a say-again escalation ladder

props.content: The request was a failure/remediation pipeline: say again once, escalate to a model on the second miss, everything configurable per environment and flight. The investigation found something better than a new system to build — the repair framework already existed inside the candidate arbitration layer, gated by policy, with budgets and telemetry. It was just welded shut: the order of repair strategies was a fixed code sequence, providers were constructed from a hardcoded tuple, and turning anything on, off, or around meant editing Python. So the foundation work became: make the existing pipeline instantiable from config, byte-for-byte identical, so every future remediation experiment is a YAML edit instead of a refactor.

props.label: THE FINDING
props.title: The pipeline was already the framework

props.content:
Every utterance segment gets a **raw parse** from the regex cascade — the most-trusted candidate, trust tier zero. Then repair sources compete to displace it: template ASR cleanup, generated strict templates, fuzzy row hints, a fine-tuned qwen structured parser, the grammar/Earley shadow lane, slot repair. A **PolicyChain** picks the winner by trust tier among policy-eligible candidates, and a YAML overlay (`CandidateSourcePolicy`) already controlled each source's mode — off, shadow (runs but can never win), or active — plus trust tiers, row scoping, and score thresholds.

What it could *not* do: change **which sources run, in what order**, or add a second pipeline with a different recipe. Three welds held it shut — the candidate build sequence hardcoded inside `arbitrate_segment_candidates`, the provider tuple hardcoded in `pipeline_factory`, and DeBERTa's disabled state expressed as a constructor branch instead of a config fact.
Isn't this kinda just the same pipeline we have with candidates? — the hunch that redirected the whole effort. It was 80% right; the missing 20% was config, not code.

props.label: THE CHANGE
props.title: One list in YAML replaced three welds in Python
Before
props.content: Candidate sources ran in a fixed inline sequence inside a 500-line function. Adding, removing, or reordering a repair strategy meant editing arbitration code and re-proving the whole surface. Providers came from a literal tuple in the factory. A second pipeline (a repair recipe, an experiment lane) required forking code paths.

props.title: After
props.content: The overlay's `candidate_source_order` list is the single dispatch truth. Arbitration walks it; the factory instantiates providers from a registry by walking the same list; validation fails closed at overlay load and daemon startup — unknown source, missing raw, duplicates, or an empty order can never reach a live turn. A second pipeline is now one more overlay document through the same loader.

props.label: METHOD
props.title: Five slices, each provably inert
props.subtitle: Every slice was gated on determinism (baseline-self-parity, 1539 rows run twice) and a row-for-row baseline diff. Workers' claims were replayed independently; two 'pre-existing failure' claims were verified by control experiments before acceptance.

props.title: 1 · Lock
props.content: Regression tests froze today's behavior first — the exact candidate order, the per-source candidate_index (build-order-assigned and load-bearing in evidence), and trace emission order.

props.title: 2 · Declare
props.content: The order list shipped in YAML with fail-closed loader validation — parsed by everything, consumed by nothing. Pure inert config.

props.title: 3 · Extract
props.content: The inline blocks became step functions over a shared state object — same literal call sequence, zero semantic change. The riskiest diff, covered by slice 1's locks.

props.title: 4 · Consume
props.content: Dispatch loops over the YAML order; providers build from a registry; startup validation fails the daemon at boot, never mid-turn. A permuted-order test proves config actually drives behavior.

props.title: 5 · Freeze
props.content: DeBERTa's absence became a locked config fact: no adapter under the config path, and an architecture-fitness test that fails on any new construction call site.

props.label: PAYOFF
props.title: What this unlocks
props.subtitle: The original three-step plan is now mostly configuration.

props.title: 🧪 The repair pipeline is one YAML file
props.content: The staged qwen repair design (deterministic evidence retrieval for 4 failure classes, model-planned retrieval for no-intent, all shadow) plugs in as a second overlay document through the same loader — no arbitration changes. That lane was notified it's unblocked.

props.title: 🎚️ Stages become experiments
props.content: Add, remove, reorder, or A/B a remediation strategy by editing a list — with shadow mode, per-source budgets, and would-have-won telemetry already in place to score it.

props.title: 🚫 Disable-don't-delete, enforced
props.content: DeBERTa (or any source) exists in a pipeline only if its config says so. Reviving it as a validator someday is a config discussion, not an archaeology project — and new call sites fail CI today.

props.title: 🗺️ Per-recipe pipelines
props.content: Different overlay documents can define different recipes — the seam for the phase-2/phase-3 clarification behaviors and for named environment profiles, without a config-matrix explosion.

props.label: TRUST
props.title: Why we believe it changed nothing
props.subtitle: The claim 'byte-identical, just relocated wiring' is load-bearing — here is its evidence.

props.content:
**Determinism gate**: `baseline-self-parity` ran green after every slice — two full 1539-row scorecard runs, deep-diffed, zero non-timing differences.

**Row-for-row diffs**: full baseline captured before and after the risky slices; the one non-zero diff (496 rows) was forensically decomposed — 473 rows from a degraded capture (B-runner timeout under load) and 23 rows whose only changes were grammar shadow telemetry with zero pass/fail movement, the exact fingerprint of a *parallel session* promoting grammar candidate_ids mid-window. Verified by inspecting their overlay edit directly.

**Control experiments**: both times a worker claimed 'those failures are pre-existing,' the claim was tested by stashing the changes and re-running — identical failure counts without our code both times.

**Full-pipeline gate**: final-boss ran end-to-end on live audio — 23 of 25 gates green, 356 turns, zero timeouts, p50 322ms. The two red gates diff back to FMM-lane and radio-lane drift accumulated over ten days of parallel work, already routed to their owning lanes with the evidence attached.

props.label: AROUND IT
props.title: The decisions that shaped the same two days
props.subtitle: The pipeline work was the build lane; these settled what gets built on top.

props.title: 📊 Failure modes, measured
props.content: 103 failing rows classified into six classes. The decisive finding: regex confidence is hardcoded 1.0, and the worst failures — 31 confident-but-wrong parses — are invisible to any retry ladder. Detected failures get the ladder; undetected ones need a disagreement/validator lane. The 31 rows are now a labeled eval set.

props.title: 📦 Turn state as blackbox events
props.content: Decision: no FSM hosted in a daemon. Cross-turn clarification state is data beside flight tracker state — append-only events per flight, counters as folds, FMM payloads captured, transitions validated by the FSM's table as a library. Ratification requested from the blackbox lane.

props.title: 🎛️ Phase-2 confidence, honestly
props.content: The demo's 'readback given a confidence level' gets a composite deterministic band (disagreement + slot completeness + coverage), per segment — the seam for phase-3 partial-compound clarification. Pre-declared eval against the 31-row set is running; if it can't beat chance, the demo ships plain readback with no decoration.
